analysis.one_liner: Bars nursing homes and home-care providers from forcing residents into pre-dispute arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in April 2024, where it died without a hearing, a markup, or any vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Nursing homes and home-care providers often ask new residents or patients to sign an arbitration agreement as part of admission paperwork. Signing means that if the resident is later neglected, abused, or otherwise harmed, the family cannot sue in court and must take the case to a private arbitrator chosen under the provider's rules. This bill would make those agreements invalid and unenforceable for Medicare and Medicaid nursing facilities, home- and community-based services, and home health care — including agreements already signed — and would keep disputes decided by courts instead.
analysis.who_benefits: Nursing home residents and home-care patients covered by Medicare or Medicaid, and their families, who would keep the right to take injury, neglect, or wrongful-death claims to a public court with a judge, jury, and public record instead of a private arbitration process.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nursing home residents and their families

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits skilled nursing facilities and Medicaid nursing facilities from requiring, soliciting, accepting, or seeking to enforce pre-dispute arbitration agreements with residents, and declares such agreements invalid and unenforceable against current and former residents, including those signed before the bill's effective date.
The bill extends the same protection to people receiving home- and community-based services and home health care under Medicaid, covering the provider, its employees, agents, and affiliates.
The bill requires that questions about whether and how the arbitration ban applies be decided by a court under federal law, rather than by an arbitrator.

analysis.who_pays: Nursing facilities, home-care providers, and arbitration service providers lose a tool that keeps liability claims out of court. Facilities argue arbitration keeps disputes cheaper and faster, so some of that cost could show up in operating expenses — though most facilities' revenues are set by Medicare and Medicaid payment rates.

drawbacks.text: Providers contend that arbitration is faster and less expensive than litigation, and that resolving every injury claim in court raises their costs; since most facility revenue comes from Medicare and Medicaid rates, some of that cost could ultimately be borne by the programs that pay for care.
The bill applies retroactively: agreements already signed would be voided, which goes beyond simply stopping the practice going forward and could reopen settled or pending disputes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For residents and families, the benefit is direct: access to open court for abuse, neglect, and wrongful-death claims, where proceedings are public and damages are not capped by private contract. The costs fall on providers and the arbitration industry, and the honest tradeoff is that litigation can be slower and costlier than arbitration — but arbitration agreements are typically signed at admission, often under pressure, by people or families in no position to negotiate. The scale of the benefit to the public clearly outweighs the cost to providers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Blumenthal introduced the bill in the Senate on April 9, 2024, joined by Sen. Mazie Hirono.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action appears in the bill's history: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing facilities, home-care providers, and arbitration firms are better off because the bill never moved: they keep the ability to route injury and wrongful-death claims into private arbitration rather than open court. Residents and families remain subject to the agreements the bill would have voided.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fairness in Nursing Home Arbitration Act in the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Mazie Hirono
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — during the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican signed on; but with only two senators behind the bill and no committee or floor action, the record shows too little activity to establish a partisan fight.

industries.note: The bill would bar these providers from requiring pre-dispute arbitration agreements, exposing them to jury trials and public court proceedings for abuse, neglect, and wrongful-death claims — including claims under agreements already signed. For residents, admission-time arbitration clauses close off the most public and accountable forum for the worst outcomes.
Arbitration firms collect fees on nursing home and home-care disputes; the bill would remove a block of that caseload and shift disputes back to courts.
